subtitle: Law and money, and the same word on three levels
words.intro: A German small-claims court is calm, wood-panelled and almost empty. People take their neighbours there over very small sums, and for the principle. Here a word is chosen with care: you *get* a letter at home, but in court you *receive* it.

grammar[0].fact: In German the verb comes with the noun, and it must be the right one. You *reichst eine Klage ein*, you *legst Berufung ein*, and you *meldest Insolvenz an*. Say *machen* with any of them, and your lawyer will look out of the window.

grammar[1].blocks[1].root.q: Is it long, Latin or with be-, ver-, er-, ent-?
grammar[1].fact: Most German words at this level come in sets of three: *kriegen, bekommen, erhalten*; *anfangen, beginnen, einleiten*; *kaputt, defekt, beschädigt*. None of them is wrong. Your skill lies in which one you pick, and who is listening.

document.intro: A real summons from a Swiss court of April 1926. A woman has to appear as a witness in a divorce case. Look at how far the language can stand from the person: *erlässt hiemit unter Androhung der gesetzlichen Folgen*.
document.fact: Under the printed words is a real, small drama: a Saturday morning in court, and a neighbour or relative who has to tell what she knows. Swiss official German still has its own forms. *Hiemit* for *hiermit* has been out of fashion in Germany for a long time.

reading.intro: The property company has charged Frau Huber 14.20 euros too much for the caretaker. She has objected, appealed and filed a claim. The lawyer’s fees are now at about 900 euros. Max has been called as a witness, and he has been told to speak properly.
reading.fact: Germans are among the keenest legal insurance customers in Europe, and suing a neighbour costs them little more than the premium. Disputes about hedges, noise and service charges fill the local courts. In many places you must first try a mediator, called a *Schiedsperson*.
